rv.q: After wobbling in tone and pace, the production pops to life in its much briefer second act, a straightforwardly silly travesty of 'Thérèse Raquin.'
But even a tasty dessert can't rescue a pallid main course.
Thirty years later, the play still feels subversive, witty, and even eerily relevant.
Luckily, the audience of The Artificial Jungle is likely to suffer a more enjoyable fate: Death by laughter.
They know how to turn artifice into rollicking laughter.
The fact that Ludlam could turn such a deadly scenario into a platform for his hilarious designs is nothing less than astonishing.
It surprised my inpatient mind with plenty of amusement once it got rolling, though it needed to percolate a little sooner.
Much of this can be humorous but it no longer packs the comic punch it had in 1986.
The Artificial Jungle mixes all human emotions into a stew of wonderful theater.
The hilarious, campy style of Charles Ludlam and the Ridiculous Theatrical Company lives on, in this excellent revival.
It is goofy, farcical and very funny. The play, by the prolific Charles Ludlam, is loud and preposterous but doesn't fall to slapstick.
This revival is a welcome reminder of the brilliance of Charles Ludlam.

For a fun evening of silly entertainment, you might want to head on out to the Theater Breaking Through Barriers' revival of Charles Ludlam's film noir parody, The Artificial Jungle, at the Clurman Theatre at Theatre Row.

cn.t: Critics largely embrace this campy Ludlam revival as silly, riotous fun, though some find the first act wobbles before hitting its stride. The absurdist noir parody divides on execution, but most celebrate its ridiculous spirit.
